nonAffiliation: These are our own practice questions. They are not the official test questions, and this app is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by the Government of Canada or Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. Canada does not publish the real question pool, so nobody has it.
disclosure: Canada does not publish the questions used in the citizenship test, so these are practice questions we wrote ourselves. Every one of them tests a fact stated in Discover Canada: The Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship, the free official study guide, and records the chapter it came from so you can check it. IRCC's own advice is that the official guide is the only official study guide and should be your primary resource - it is free, and we link to every chapter.

questions.question: Canada's tradition of ordered liberty is usually traced back to the signing of which document?
options: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Magna Carta, signed in England in 1215
answers: Magna Carta, signed in England in 1215

questions.question: Which right lets a person challenge unlawful detention by the state?
In which year was the Constitution amended to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
Which of these is a fundamental freedom protected in Canada?
options: The right to carry a weapon
The right to a government job

questions.question: What do mobility rights give Canadians?
options: The right to live and work anywhere in Canada, and to enter and leave the country freely
The right to move to any other country
The right to change province without telling any government
The right to free public transport
answers: The right to live and work anywhere in Canada, and to enter and leave the country freely

questions.question: Which of these is a responsibility of Canadian citizenship?
options: Serving on a jury when called to do so
answers: Serving on a jury when called to do so

questions.question: What does Canadian law say about military service?
options: There is no compulsory military service in Canada
Every citizen must serve for two years
Service is compulsory in wartime only
answers: There is no compulsory military service in Canada

questions.question: Under Canadian law, what is the status of men and women?
options: Men have priority in family matters
It is decided by each community
Men and women are equal under the law
answers: Men and women are equal under the law

questions.question: What does the responsibility of 'obeying the law' rest on?
options: The discretion of the Prime Minister
The will of the majority in each town
The rule of law, under which no person or group is above the law
answers: The rule of law, under which no person or group is above the law

questions.question: Which of these is named in the guide as a citizenship responsibility?
What are the three key facts about Canada's system of government?
options: It is a republic, a direct democracy and a federation
It is a unitary state, a presidential democracy and a monarchy
It is a confederation, a republic and a parliamentary democracy
It is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
answers: It is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy

questions.question: What are the three parts of Parliament?
options: The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
The House of Commons, the Supreme Court and the Senate
The Governor General, the Prime Minister and the House of Commons
The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the Senate
answers: The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons

questions.question: Which Act of 1867 defined the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments?
options: The British North America Act, now known as the Constitution Act, 1867
answers: The British North America Act, now known as the Constitution Act, 1867

questions.question: Which of these is a federal responsibility?
Which of these is a provincial responsibility?
Which two areas do the federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction over?
How do senators take their seats, and how long do they serve?
options: They are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister, and serve until age 75
They are chosen by the provincial legislatures for life
They are elected at the same time as members of the House of Commons
They are elected for a fixed term of eight years
answers: They are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister, and serve until age 75

questions.question: Who grants royal assent to a bill, and on whose behalf?
options: The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The Prime Minister, on behalf of Parliament
The Governor General, on behalf of the Sovereign
answers: The Governor General, on behalf of the Sovereign

questions.question: What must happen before a bill becomes law in Canada?
options: It must be passed by both the House of Commons and the Senate, and receive royal assent
It must be approved in a national referendum
It must be passed by the House of Commons alone
It must be signed by the Prime Minister
answers: It must be passed by both the House of Commons and the Senate, and receive royal assent

questions.question: In Canada's constitutional monarchy, what does the Sovereign reign in accordance with?
options: The Constitution, and so the rule of law
The instructions of the Prime Minister
The advice of the Supreme Court
A vote of the House of Commons
answers: The Constitution, and so the rule of law

questions.question: What happens to Cabinet ministers who are defeated in a non-confidence vote?
options: They are appointed to the Senate
Nothing; the vote is only advisory
They may stay in office for one more year

questions.question: Under legislation passed by Parliament, when must a federal election be held?
options: In the spring of every fifth year
On the first Tuesday in November every four years
On the third Monday in October every four years after the most recent general election
answers: On the third Monday in October every four years after the most recent general election

questions.question: Who may ask the Governor General to call an earlier election?
What are the three requirements to vote in a federal election?
options: Being born in Canada, being 18, and having a passport
Being a resident of Canada, being 21, and owning property
Being a Canadian citizen, speaking English or French, and paying taxes
Being a Canadian citizen, being at least 18 on voting day, and being on the voters' list
answers: Being a Canadian citizen, being at least 18 on voting day, and being on the voters' list

questions.question: What is an electoral district also known as?
In each electoral district, which candidate becomes the member of Parliament?
options: The candidate who receives more than half of all votes
The candidate whose party wins nationally
The candidate who receives the most votes
The candidate chosen by the outgoing MP
answers: The candidate who receives the most votes

questions.question: Which neutral agency of Parliament produces the voters' lists?
What is a majority government?
options: One where the party in power won the most votes nationally
One formed by two or more parties together
One where the party in power holds at least half of the seats in the House of Commons
One where the party in power holds fewer than half of the seats
answers: One where the party in power holds at least half of the seats in the House of Commons

questions.question: What does the right to a secret ballot mean?
options: Only election officers may know your name
You must not discuss politics on election day
No one can watch you vote and no one has the right to insist you say how you voted
answers: No one can watch you vote and no one has the right to insist you say how you voted

questions.question: After an election, who is ordinarily invited to form the government?
options: The leader of the party with the most votes nationally
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The leader of the party with the most seats in the House of Commons
answers: The leader of the party with the most seats in the House of Commons

questions.question: What is the Official Opposition?
options: The opposition party with the most members in the House of Commons
A committee of senators who review government bills
Any party that voted against the budget
answers: The opposition party with the most members in the House of Commons

questions.question: In which year was a new Canadian flag raised for the first time?
Where does the red-white-red pattern of the Canadian flag come from?
options: The flag of the Royal Military College in Kingston
The flag of the Hudson's Bay Company
answers: The flag of the Royal Military College in Kingston

questions.question: Since when have red and white been the national colours of Canada?
Which flag is Canada's official Royal Flag?
options: The flag of the Royal Military College

questions.question: What is Canada's best-known symbol?
What does Canada's national motto, A Mari Usque Ad Mare, mean?
When did Canada adopt an official coat of arms and a national motto?
options: When the new flag was raised in 1965
When the Constitution was amended in 1982
As an expression of national pride after the First World War
answers: As an expression of national pride after the First World War

questions.question: In which year did Quebec adopt its own flag, based on the Cross and the fleur-de-lys?
Which institutions is the Crown a symbol of?
options: The Senate and the House of Commons only
Parliament, the legislatures, the courts, police services and the Canadian Forces
Only the monarchy and the Governor General
answers: Parliament, the legislatures, the courts, police services and the Canadian Forces

questions.question: During whose reign did Canada become a constitutional monarchy in its own right, at Confederation?
Who was the first to map Canada's Atlantic shore, in 1497?
Who built a fortress in 1608 at what is now Quebec City?
In which year did the French and the Iroquois make peace?
Why did the British Parliament pass the Quebec Act of 1774?
options: To unite Upper and Lower Canada
To abolish slavery in the colonies
To better govern the French Roman Catholic majority
To create the Dominion of Canada
answers: To better govern the French Roman Catholic majority

questions.question: Where and when was the first representative assembly in what is now Canada elected?
In which year did the British Parliament abolish slavery throughout the Empire?
Which country launched an invasion of Canada in June 1812?
What was the outcome of the War of 1812 for Canada?
options: Canada was annexed by the United States
Upper and Lower Canada were united
Britain gave up its North American colonies
The American attempt to conquer Canada failed, and Canada remained independent of the United States
answers: The American attempt to conquer Canada failed, and Canada remained independent of the United States

questions.question: In 1840, Upper and Lower Canada were united as what?
Which was the first British North American colony to attain full responsible government?
On what date was the Dominion of Canada officially born?
Who suggested the term 'Dominion of Canada' in 1864?
What is the capital city of Ontario?
What is the capital city of Quebec?
What is the capital city of Nova Scotia?
What is the capital city of British Columbia?
What is the capital city of Alberta?
What is the capital city of Manitoba?
What is the capital city of Saskatchewan?
What is the capital city of Newfoundland and Labrador?
What is the capital city of New Brunswick?
What is the capital city of Prince Edward Island?
What is the capital city of Nunavut?
What is the capital city of the Northwest Territories?
What is the capital city of Yukon?
Which four provinces make up the Atlantic region?
options: Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario
Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Nova Scotia
Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec
answers: Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick

questions.question: Which three provinces are the Prairie Provinces?
options: Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories

questions.question: Which two provinces make up Central Canada?
What is the Canadian justice system founded on in criminal matters?
options: The presumption of innocence - everyone is innocent until proven guilty
answers: The presumption of innocence - everyone is innocent until proven guilty

questions.question: Which is Canada's highest court?
What does the Federal Court of Canada deal with?
What is due process?
options: The principle that government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law
The requirement that laws be published before they take effect
The rule that trials must finish within a year
The right to a jury in every case
answers: The principle that government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law

questions.question: Who does the law in Canada apply to?
options: Everyone except members of Parliament while in session
Everyone, including judges, politicians and the police
answers: Everyone, including judges, politicians and the police

questions.question: In the Oath of Citizenship, to whom does a new citizen bear true allegiance?
options: His Majesty King Charles the Third, King of Canada
answers: His Majesty King Charles the Third, King of Canada

questions.question: As well as allegiance, what does the Oath of Citizenship now refer to?
options: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Aboriginal and treaty rights of Indigenous peoples in Canada
answers: Aboriginal and treaty rights of Indigenous peoples in Canada
